specStatements.text: The test for hydrogen uses a burning splint held at the open end of a test tube of the gas. Hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.
The test for oxygen uses a glowing splint inserted into a test tube of the gas. The splint relights in oxygen.
The test for carbon dioxide uses an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide (lime water). When carbon dioxide is shaken with or bubbled through limewater the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
The test for chlorine uses litmus paper. When damp litmus paper is put into chlorine gas the litmus paper is bleached and turns white.

concepts.definition: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of the gas; hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.
A wooden splint that has been lit so it carries a flame; it is held at the open end of the test tube in the hydrogen test.
The short, sharp squeak heard as hydrogen burns rapidly at the mouth of the test tube; it is the positive result for hydrogen.
A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of the gas; the splint relights in oxygen.
A splint that has been lit and then blown out, so the tip is still glowing red hot but carries no flame.
The glowing tip of the splint bursts back into flame when it is inserted into oxygen; this is the positive result for oxygen.
An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide, used as the test reagent for carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide is shaken with or bubbled through limewater; the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
The white, opaque appearance limewater takes on when carbon dioxide is passed through it; it is the positive result for carbon dioxide.
Damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas; the litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
Litmus paper moistened with water before it is put into the gas; the chlorine test uses damp, not dry, litmus paper.
The colour of the litmus paper is removed so that the paper turns white; this is the positive result for chlorine.

misconceptions.question: What does hydrogen do to a glowing splint?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen is identified with a burning splint and a pop sound; relighting a glowing splint is the oxygen result.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think hydrogen relights a glowing splint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both tests use a wooden splint, so the two procedures and their results are swapped in memory.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the pairs together: burning splint plus pop is hydrogen; glowing splint plus relight is oxygen.

misconceptions.question: What happens to a burning splint held at the open end of a tube of hydrogen?
misconceptions.correct: The hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think the splint is simply put out, because the tube contains no oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They over-apply the rule that a flame needs oxygen and forget that the hydrogen itself burns in the air at the mouth of the tube.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen is the flammable gas here; it burns rapidly at the open end and the pop is heard.

misconceptions.question: Which splint is used to test for oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: A glowing splint, which relights in the gas.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think the oxygen test uses a burning splint.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A burning splint is the more familiar piece of practical work, and a splint burning more brightly in oxygen looks like a sensible result.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the oxygen test uses a glowing splint inserted into the tube, and that the splint relights.

misconceptions.question: Does the oxygen itself burn when the splint relights?
misconceptions.correct: No. The splint burns; the oxygen supports that burning.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think oxygen is a flammable gas that catches fire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words fire, burning and oxygen are used together so often that oxygen gets labelled as the fuel.
misconceptions.correction: Oxygen supports combustion; the fuel in this test is the wooden splint.

misconceptions.question: What solute is dissolved in limewater?
misconceptions.correct: Calcium hydroxide; limewater is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think limewater is sodium hydroxide solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali met most often in class, so any alkaline solution is assumed to be that one.
misconceptions.correction: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution: the calcium is what forms the milky solid when carbon dioxide is added.

misconceptions.question: Is limewater a solution of calcium carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think limewater is calcium carbonate solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They remember calcium carbonate from this test and confuse the insoluble product with the starting reagent.
misconceptions.correction: Calcium hydroxide is the dissolved reagent; the calcium carbonate formed is insoluble, which is why the solution goes cloudy.

misconceptions.question: What happens to limewater when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it?
misconceptions.misconception: Students think there is no visible change because carbon dioxide is a colourless gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: They expect a colourless gas to give a colourless result, and think a positive test must mean a new colour.
misconceptions.correction: The change is not a colour change but a cloudiness: a white insoluble solid forms and makes the limewater milky.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide relight a glowing splint?
misconceptions.correct: No. Carbon dioxide puts a glowing splint out; oxygen relights it.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think a glowing splint relights in carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide and oxygen are the two gases tested most often, so the observation is attached to the wrong one.
misconceptions.correction: Only oxygen relights the glowing splint; carbon dioxide is identified by limewater turning milky.

misconceptions.question: Does carbon dioxide bleach limewater white?
misconceptions.correct: No. It makes the limewater milky; bleaching to white is the chlorine result on litmus paper.
misconceptions.misconception: Students describe the limewater as being bleached white.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Milky and white sound like the same observation, so the carbon dioxide result is described in the language of the chlorine test.
misconceptions.correction: Limewater turns milky or cloudy because a white solid forms in it; nothing is bleached.

misconceptions.question: What colour is damp litmus paper after it is put into chlorine gas?
misconceptions.correct: White, because the paper is bleached.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think the paper simply turns red and stays red.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper to give an acidic solution, so a red colour can be seen first and students stop the observation there.
misconceptions.correction: The specification result is that damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white.

misconceptions.question: Does chlorine turn litmus paper blue?
misconceptions.correct: No. The litmus paper is bleached and turns white.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think chlorine is alkaline and so turns litmus blue.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Household bleach is an alkaline product associated with chlorine, so the alkali label is transferred to the gas.
misconceptions.correction: The chlorine test result is a loss of colour to white, not a blue colour.

misconceptions.question: Can dry litmus paper be used to test for chlorine?
misconceptions.correct: No. The test uses damp litmus paper.
misconceptions.misconception: Students think dry litmus paper gives the same white result.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word damp is treated as an unimportant practical detail rather than part of the stated test.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas and is bleached.

mcqs.stem: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of an unknown gas. Which observation shows that the gas is hydrogen?

options.text: The gas burns rapidly with a pop sound
options.rationale: This is the stated result of the hydrogen test: hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.

options.text: The splint relights, burning brightly
options.rationale: This is the oxygen result, chosen by students who swap the two splint tests.

options.text: The splint is put out straight away
options.rationale: Students who think a flame always needs oxygen expect any other gas to extinguish it.

options.text: The gas burns with a steady flame
options.rationale: Students know hydrogen is flammable but forget that the identifying observation is rapid burning with a pop.

mcqs.stem: Which procedure and result together make up the test for hydrogen?

options.text: A glowing splint is inserted and then relights
options.rationale: This is the oxygen test written out in full; students who swap the splints choose it.

options.text: Damp litmus paper is held in it and whitens
options.rationale: This is the chlorine test, picked by students who match any gas to any test.

options.text: A burning splint at the open end gives a pop
options.rationale: The test uses a burning splint held at the open end of the tube, and hydrogen burns rapidly with a pop sound.

options.text: A burning splint at the open end goes out
options.rationale: Students who think the tube holds no oxygen expect the flame to be extinguished rather than a pop.

mcqs.stem: A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of gas and the splint relights. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The gas is carbon dioxide, as it relights splints
options.rationale: Students attach the relighting observation to the other gas they test most often.

options.text: The gas is oxygen, as it relights the splint
options.rationale: The splint relights in oxygen, so relighting identifies the gas as oxygen.

options.text: The relighting shows the gas is burning itself
options.rationale: Students who label oxygen as flammable read the flame as the gas catching fire, not the splint burning.

options.text: The gas is hydrogen, as it relights splints
options.rationale: Students who swap the two splint tests expect hydrogen to relight a glowing splint.

mcqs.stem: Which splint and which result are used to identify oxygen?

options.text: A burning splint that then relights
options.rationale: Students remember the relighting but pair it with the more familiar burning splint.

options.text: A glowing splint that lights the gas
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the oxygen itself is the fuel that burns.

options.text: A burning splint that gives a pop
options.rationale: This is the hydrogen result, chosen when the two gas tests are matched the wrong way round.

options.text: A glowing splint that relights
options.rationale: The oxygen test inserts a glowing splint into the tube and the splint relights.

mcqs.stem: Limewater is used in the test for carbon dioxide. What is limewater?

options.text: An aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide
options.rationale: Sodium hydroxide is the alkali met most often, so it is assumed to be the one in limewater.

options.text: An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide
options.rationale: The specification defines limewater as an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.

options.text: An aqueous calcium carbonate solution
options.rationale: Students confuse the insoluble product of the test with the reagent used in it.

options.text: An aqueous calcium chloride solution
options.rationale: A plausible calcium salt for students who recall only that limewater contains calcium.

mcqs.stem: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. What is observed?

options.text: The limewater turns a bright yellow
options.rationale: Students who expect a positive test to mean a new colour choose a colour change.

options.text: The limewater is bleached white
options.rationale: Milky and white sound alike, so chlorine language is used for the carbon dioxide result.

options.text: The limewater stays unchanged
options.rationale: Students expect a colourless gas to leave a colourless solution looking the same.

options.text: The limewater turns milky (cloudy)
options.rationale: The stated result is that the limewater turns milky (cloudy).

mcqs.stem: Damp litmus paper is put into a test tube of chlorine gas. What happens to the paper?

options.text: It turns bright red and stays red
options.rationale: Students stop at the acidic colour change and never record the loss of colour.

options.text: It turns green like the gas
options.rationale: Students assume the pale green gas simply dyes the paper its own colour.

options.text: It is bleached and turns white
options.rationale: The stated result is that the damp litmus paper is bleached and turns white.

options.text: It turns blue, showing an alkali
options.rationale: Bleach is thought of as alkaline, so chlorine is expected to turn litmus blue.

mcqs.stem: Which observation identifies a gas as chlorine?

options.text: Damp litmus paper turns white
options.rationale: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper, so the paper turns white.

options.text: Dry litmus paper turns bright white
options.rationale: Students treat damp as an optional detail and accept dry paper for the test.

options.text: Damp litmus paper turns deep red
options.rationale: Students record only the acidic change and leave out the bleaching.

options.text: Limewater goes cloudy and milky
options.rationale: This is the carbon dioxide result, chosen when gas tests are matched at random.
